opening.headline: In a service where both up-to-date information and source attribution are required, it distinguishes how web grounding and citation operate and where they can be trusted.
body: The model only has knowledge up to the point when training ended. However, users ask about today's prices or content released yesterday. Even if the model provides the correct answer, without a source, the user has no basis to trust it, and it becomes difficult to verify where the answer might be incorrect if it is wrong.

In this lesson, we examine the operational mechanism of web grounding—where a model searches the web to find answers—and the structure of citations that link search results to responses with their sources. We then explore examples of how to assess source-level trustworthiness when combining internal documents and web information, and how to handle conflicts between two sources.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of web grounding and citation of search results
Can distinguish trust boundaries when combining internal documents and web information, and establish a conflict resolution order.

screens.title: Latest information and source citations are both required.
screens.lead: Consider the following scenario and think about why the correct answer might differ from what is believable.

visual.alt: A scene where answers to a user's today's price query are displayed side by side, one without a source and the other with a source for comparison.
labels: What is today's sale price for this product?
[1] Official pricing information page, verify today

paragraphs: In customer service, a user asks: "What is today's sales figure for this product, and what policy was announced yesterday?" Since the model does not know events occurring after the training phase, it may provide outdated values or fabricate plausible responses without any actual device or data to reference.

Even if luck is good and the answer is correct, a problem remains. Without a source, users have no basis to trust the answer, and agents cannot trace where the information came from if the answer is wrong. Services that require up-to-date information need both a device to retrieve the information and a device that shows where the information originated.

The preceding device is web grounding, and the following device is citation. This course addresses the issue of trust that arises when combining the structure of both devices, internal documentation, and web information.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If information obtained from the web has a source cited, can we trust that information? We will summarize the relationship between sources and trust at the end of the class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall how my service ensures up-to-date functionality.

screens.title: Think about how freshness of responses is ensured
screens.lead: When you select a method, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you haven't entered or submitted an answer, first consider which method you'd use in your service.

items.prompt: How do you directly insert recent materials into the prompt?
items.answer: The simplest and most reliable approach is that human beings must prepare and update the data. This method can only be used when it's possible in advance to know which data is needed for a particular question, and the cost of data entry increases as the data becomes more extensive.

items.prompt: How do I periodically re-index internal documents?
items.answer: Our organization can manage the timeliness of its information using this method. A clear assignment of document ownership and responsibility for updates is a benefit. However, changes in the external world—such as today's market prices or yesterday's announcements—are not reflected in internal documents.

items.prompt: How can a model be made to search the web directly?
items.answer: This is appropriate for retrieving the latest information from the external world. When the model determines that a search is necessary, it performs the search, uses the results to formulate a response, and provides the source alongside the answer. However, since the quality of web sources varies, a policy for selecting which sources to use is required. This is the central topic of this course.

screens.outro: We will look at how web grounding actually works step by step.

screens.title: Web grounding operation: the model decides the search.
screens.lead: Select the arrow and proceed step by step through the flow of the request processing sequence, following the workflow that includes a web search tool.

visual.alt: A cyclic flow from user query to model judgment, search execution, result delivery, and the final response with citations.
labels: Search: Latest news, current price, changing information
Search disabled: Mathematics, Science fundamentals, analysis of provided content, creation

steps.title: 1. Insert the search tool into the request
steps.body: Developers add a web search tool to the list of available tools in the request. Claude uses the web_search tool, Gemini uses the google_search tool, and OpenAI uses the web_search tool from the Responses API. Developers do not need to repeatedly check whether to include a search tool; the model determines whether to perform a search based on analyzing the user's question.

steps.title: 2. The model determines whether to perform a search.
steps.body: According to the Claude document, searches are performed when the request depends on current, evolving, or out-of-learning-range information. This includes recent news or announcements, current prices and statistics, information about organizations or products that may have changed, and explicit requests to search. Conversely, queries related to mathematical, scientific fundamentals, coding concepts, creative tasks, or analysis of already provided content are answered directly without searching.

steps.title: 3. The API performs the search and returns the results.
steps.body: If the model determines that a search is needed, the API executes the search and provides the results to the model. This process can be repeated multiple times within a single request. A cap such as max_uses can be set on the number of searches, and the system prompt can be used to regulate excessive searching.

steps.title: 4. Final response with source citation
steps.body: The model responds with the last cited source. Each sentence in the response is linked to its corresponding source, allowing users to verify it directly. Gemini documents also explain the grounding effect in terms of improved factual accuracy, real-time information access, and source attribution. The three companies have different names but provide the same structure.

screens.outro: We will verify the structure of the search result block that forms the foundation of the citation in code.

screens.title: Structure of Search Results Block and Citation Attribution
screens.lead: The following is a search_result block based on Claude, containing source material passed to it. Selecting emphasized sections allows you to see the role each field plays within the citation.

marks.note: This is a required field. It should be a stable string that points to a source, such as a web address or an internal document identifier like kb://. Since this value is directly included in the citation, it must be a value that allows users to trace back the source.

This is a required field. It should be a title describing the result, and it should be included with the citation and source. If the title is ambiguous, users will not know which document is being referenced.

marks.span: The basic plan costs 12,000 won per month.
marks.note: This is a text block within the content array of required fields. It represents the actual content that the model relies on, and only text can be entered—images are not supported. The model selects citable sentences from this content to include in its response.

This is a selectable field with a default value of off. When enabled, the model automatically adds citations to sentences that contain this result. All search results within a single request must use the same setting. If this value is omitted, the rationale is provided but no citations are displayed.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the structure of source attribution, let's move on to the question of how much to trust a particular source.

screens.title: Trust boundary: When mixing internal documentation with web content
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the trust levels and management responsibilities by source type. On the last tab, you can verify methods for controlling the source scope.

tabs.label: Internal document
tabs.body: This document is directly managed by our organization. The authorship and update responsibility are clearly defined, making it easy to establish a trust level. It is one of the most authoritative sources among organizational-defined facts such as internal policies, contract terms, and product specifications. The weakness is that it is tied to update timing; if updates are delayed, outdated values are used as if they were current.

tabs.label: Web search results
tabs.body: While it has the advantage of being up-to-date, the quality of sources varies significantly. Official announcements, blogs, and old posts can appear together in the same search results. The fact that a source is cited only indicates the location of the evidence, not that the source itself is reliable. Therefore, you should predefine which domains' results are acceptable.

tabs.label: Model's learning memory
tabs.body: This is the rationale behind the model's response when neither search results nor internal documents are available. It is fixed at the time of training and may be outdated, with no source to cite. While it provides sufficient stability for established knowledge, it should not be used as evidence for facts that are subject to change, as this would be unsafe.

tabs.label: Source scope control
tabs.body: Claude's web search tool can narrow the search scope using allowed_domains and blocked_domains. These two settings cannot be used together; only one must be specified. The tool also supports setting a limit on the number of searches per request using max_uses, and can return results tailored to a specific user location using user_location. Together with these controls, source types' priority levels should be pre-documented as policies to enable clear decision-making in case of conflicts.

screens.outro: Let's apply this policy to a case where two sources conflict.

screens.title: Case Analysis of Conflicts Between Internal Documentation and Web Search
screens.lead: Let's examine how to handle the situation where internal documents and web information differ. Select the arrow to proceed step by step and follow the judgment sequence.

steps.title: Situation: Internal pricing differs from official announcements
steps.body: The internal price list retains the value from one month ago, and the scenario assumes that the official website notification today indicates a price change. When a user asks about the current price, the model receives information from both sources. The numerical values and dates are assumed for illustrative purposes only.

steps.title: Step 1. Conflict Detection
steps.body: First, verify the dates and sources of the two references to determine whether there is a conflict. The internal price list is from a corporate document from one month ago, while the official notice is a current formal announcement. It's not enough that the values differ; the identity of the source—who issued it and when—is crucial for subsequent judgment. If the dates match but the sources differ—for example, an official notice and a third-party blog stating different values—the authority of the source becomes the deciding factor. Skipping this verification results in a mere accidental judgment based solely on the later source encountered.

steps.title: Step 2. Apply priority policy
steps.body: Priorities should be predefined for each item. For example, facts that change externally, such as price, should take precedence over official announcements, while internal policies like refund procedures should take precedence over internal documentation. If no policy exists, the model may arbitrarily select answers, leading to different responses to the same question.

steps.title: Step 3. Clearly disclose in the response.
steps.body: Cite both sources and indicate the differences in the response. For example, according to official announcements, the current value is as such, while the internal pricing sheet shows the previous value. The user gains a basis for deciding which value to trust, and the responsible party becomes aware of the discrepancy.

steps.title: Step 4. Mark internal documents as targets for update
steps.body: A conflict indicates that internal documentation is outdated. After responding, mark the document as pending update and notify the responsible party. This process ensures that conflicts do not recur and maintains the reliability of internal documentation. Conversely, if a web result contradicts a fact defined by organizational policy, prioritize the internal documentation and question the web result. Which side takes precedence varies by item, so specify this on the policy table for each item.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: The source's credibility determines the answer's credibility.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Web grounding provides models with up-to-date information, while citations give users verifiable provenance. Since the source and title of search results form the backbone of citations, passing internal documents through the same structure results in citations that mirror the format of web results. Domain controls and query limits in web search tools narrow the scope of sources. Ultimately, determining the trustworthiness of a source rests with human-defined policies.

When returning to the first question, the fact that a source is cited only indicates the location of the evidence, not the reliability of the source. Therefore, we establish a policy in advance specifying priority levels by source type, and when conflicts arise, we transparently disclose them and update internal documentation accordingly.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The prices and dates in the text are assumptions for illustrative purposes. Allowed domains and priorities should be defined by your service's origin policy.

checks.intro: Recalling the search judgment criteria you just saw, check it for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What question is a model with a web search tool enabled most likely to execute a search for?
options: Summarize the pasted paragraph into three lines.
Compose a short poem on the theme of spring.
Tell me today's sales figure for a specific product.
checks.explain: The model determines that search is necessary for information that can change, such as recent news, current prices, and statistics. Search is not required for mathematics, content analysis, or creation.

wrong.0: Math fundamentals can be answered without searching.
wrong.1: Analysis of the provided content does not require searching.

checks.intro: Now recall the collision resolution process just explained and arrange it appropriately. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: When internal pricing (previous month's value) and web official announcements (today's updated value) conflict, please review the processing order.
items: Checks the date and source of both to detect conflicts.
Determines which source to follow based on item-specific priority policies
Cite both sources and indicate the differences in the response.
Marks this document as pending update
checks.explain: First verify the conflict, make a determination based on policy, transparently communicate the response, then update internal documentation.

glossary.def: This is a method where the model searches the web and generates responses based on the results.
A source unit consisting of source, title, and content, which serves as the basis for citation.
This citation shows the source from which the response sentence originated.
This is a line that distinguishes how much to trust each source and which one to prioritize.

misconceptions.myth: When web search is enabled, all answers are up to date.
misconceptions.fact: Search only when the model determines it is necessary. For questions that do not require searching, such as mathematics or creative tasks, no search is performed. Even when a search is conducted, the quality of the source must be independently verified.
Citation shows only the location of the source; it does not imply that the source itself is trustworthy. The reliability of a source must be assessed independently.

misconceptions.myth: Internal documents and web content have the same level of trust.
misconceptions.fact: Refresh responsibility and quality are different, so item-by-item prioritization is needed.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The source's credibility determines the answer's credibility.
Web grounding provides freshness, while citation provides verifiability.
The source and title of the search result block form the backbone of the citation.
Specifies policy-based priority when internal documents and web content conflict.
